description:
Team StellarDuo is building The Earth Information Jukebox using NASA's open Earth data, combining web development, coding, and data visualization to create an engaging experience.
We're looking for teammates with UI/UX, graphic design, storytelling, or content creation skills who are passionate about space and innovation.
summary:
NASA's Earth visualizations are beautiful, but they're silent. None of the nine we worked with has any sound, so the 2.2 billion people living with a vision impairment miss them completely.

So we built the Earth Information Jukebox, a web app that lets you hear them. Pick one, like night lights, ocean currents or lightning seen from the space station, press play, and the app turns what's on screen into music as it plays.

The idea is simple. Each colour in NASA's own legend gets its own instrument. The more of that colour on screen, the louder it plays. Brighter colours play higher notes, and when the picture changes, the beat picks up. The music stays in step with the video, to within 60 milliseconds. Nothing is random, and if data is missing, the music goes quiet instead of guessing. A short line of text tells you what you're hearing.

Our teammates' backend adds a 3D globe of natural events and an ocean and temperature series you can hear as piano and waves.

We want everyone to be able to listen to a changing planet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA's Earth visualizations into music you can hear while you watch. You choose one of nine visualizations from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, press play, and the app plays the original NASA video while it creates sound from it, live, in your browser. A small panel explains in plain words what you are hearing at each moment, such as which colour is driving which instrument.

HOW IT WORKS

About twelve times a second, the app looks at the current video frame and measures three things: how much of each colour from NASA's own legend is on screen, how bright those colours are, and how much the picture is moving. Simple, written-down rules turn these into sound:

- More of a colour makes its instrument louder.

- A brighter colour plays a higher note. We use a pentatonic scale, so notes never clash.

- More movement adds more beats, spread evenly through the bar.

- The overall amount of colour sets a soft background pad.

Each visualization has its own colour groups, taken from NASA's legend or description. In the Night Lights video, yellow shows city lights in the yearly maps, but on the change map purple means more light and orange means less, so the rules switch when the video changes section. The aerosols visualization is a still image, so the app scans it from left to right like a radar sweep, an idea inspired by NASA's Caldwell 73 sonification.

Sound and picture share one master clock based on the browser's audio clock. Every video frame reports its time, and if the two drift more than 60 milliseconds apart, the app pulls them back together. In our tests the worst gap across all eight videos was 57 ms.

BACKEND DATA

Our teammates built a backend that supplies two more data feeds. Natural events such as wildfires and storms appear as points on a 3D globe. A daily ocean and temperature series becomes music too: each day is one beat, the temperature sets the pitch of a piano note (one semitone higher for every 0.1 °C above the series median), and the ocean intensity sets how loud the waves are. The app checks every record and drops anything invalid. During the hackathon we tested this with a sample of the backend's data, and the app labels it as a sample.

WHY IT MATTERS

NASA tells many of its Earth stories through images alone. None of the nine visualizations we used has any sound, so the 2.2 billion people living with a vision impairment miss them. Sound also helps everyone notice change: a city getting brighter or a storm building is easier to remember when you hear it. We imagine the Jukebox in classrooms, science fairs, museums and on large public screens.

STAYING TRUE TO THE SCIENCE

- The NASA visualizations are never cropped or recoloured.

- Nothing is random, so the same picture always makes the same sound.

- Missing data means silence. We never fill gaps or invent values.

- We never turn a colour into a made-up number, like an exact temperature or pollution level.

- Where NASA's own pages disagree, for example on dates, the app shows the disagreement instead of picking one.

- When the camera rotates or zooms, the app explains that some changes in the sound come from the camera, not from Earth.

- A limiter caps the volume so loud moments stay comfortable.

ACCESSIBILITY

The whole app works with a keyboard, announces changes to screen readers, respects reduced-motion settings and describes every sound in text. An automated WCAG 2.1 AA scan found zero violations. Our next step is testing with blind and low-vision users.

TOOLS WE USED

Next.js, React and TypeScript for the web app; Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Motion for the interface; Tone.js and the Web Audio API for sound; Three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D globe; Zod to check incoming data; FFmpeg to make browser-friendly copies of the NASA videos; and Vitest, Playwright and axe-core for 69 automated tests.

WHAT'S NEXT

We want to connect the live backend, build a physical listening room around a 3D globe (our concept film shows the idea), test with screen-reader users and add more NASA visualizations. Adding a new one mostly means describing its colour legend.
